questions.stem: Consider this: A nephew promising to pay an uncle asks whether a promise is enforceable. The promise was made after the work was done. Which statement best states the governing legal rule?

options.text: Only payment of money can count as consideration in the present case.
A promise is supported by consideration whenever the promisor had a good reason to make it in this dispute.
Consideration requires a bargained-for exchange in which each party gives or promises something of legal value in return for the other's promise as applied here.
A promise made as a gift is enforceable because it is still a promise in this situation.

questions.explanation: Consideration is what distinguishes a bargain from a gift. The promise and the return must be linked as part of an exchange, so a benefit that was not sought in return for the promise does not qualify. Here the decisive point is bargained-for exchange, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask what each party gave in exchange for the other's promise. Keep the inquiry on bargained-for exchange.

Consideration requires a bargained-for exchange in which each party gives or promises something of legal value in return for the other's promise in the case at hand.
A promise made as a gift is enforceable because it is still a promise in the present case.

Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.

Consideration requires a bargained-for exchange in which each party gives or promises something of legal value in return for the other's promise in the case at hand.
A promise made as a gift is enforceable because it is still a promise in this dispute.

questions.explanation: Consideration is what distinguishes a bargain from a gift. The promise and the return must be linked as part of an exchange, so a benefit that was not sought in return for the promise does not qualify. Here the decisive point is bargained-for exchange, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask what each party gave in exchange for the other's promise. Keep the inquiry on bargained-for exchange.

A moral obligation to pay is the same as legal consideration on the facts given.

A promise made in recognition of a benefit already received is generally unenforceable for lack of consideration, because nothing was bargained for at the time of the promise in the present case.

questions.explanation: The timing matters. If the benefit was conferred before the promise and not requested in exchange for it, the promise is a gratuitous one, and a moral sense of obligation does not by itself supply consideration. Here the decisive point is past consideration and moral obligation, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.

Promissory estoppel may enforce a promise without consideration when the promisor should reasonably expect reliance, reliance actually occurs and enforcement is the only way to avoid injustice given the events just recounted.
Any gratuitous promise is enforceable through estoppel without more given the events just recounted.
A promisee's reliance on a promise does not matter if there is no consideration given the events just recounted.

questions.explanation: Estoppel is an equitable alternative with its own elements.
